headline: WHEAT LEADS THE WEEK; CORN PRICED FOR HARVEST
subheadline: Chicago wheat closed up 22 cents Friday, beans followed, and December corn held $5.37 as combines roll toward the Belt.
lead: Wheat ended the week at $7.67, up 22 cents Friday on heat-driven supply stress, the biggest one-day move in the complex. Beans tagged along at $12.76, near a 52-week high. The story this week: the August WASDE cut yields, the Pro Farmer tour confirmed stress, and December corn at $5.37 is pricing a tighter crop. The question now is whether September has a reason to add to that premium.
the_takeaway: December corn at $5.37 already prices a tighter crop; September WASDE decides if the market paid enough.
teaser: Wheat ran 22 cents Friday, beans held near 52-week highs, and harvest is two weeks out. Here is where everything stands.

one_number.unit: of Nebraska reporting drought stress this week
one_number.context: The warm, dry pattern that accelerated late-season dough and dent stress did not ease heading into Labor Day. Drought is now a harvest-risk story, not just a yield story: combines may move fast through thin stands, but basis will tell you what the elevator already knows.

sections.title: GRAINS: WHEAT LEADS, BEANS HOLD
sections.body:
- Chicago wheat closed at **$7.67**, up 22 cents Friday and up more than 30 cents on the week; the heat-and-supply rally followed through, with Qatar LNG force majeure through November adding freight-cost anxiety.
- November beans settled at **$12.88**, near the top of their 52-week range; meal up 2.8% and oil up 1.7% Friday confirmed the Pro Farmer pod-fill stress that USDA's 52.7 bu/acre yield already flagged.
- December corn closed at **$5.365**, holding the week's gains without adding conviction; basis is the tell now as harvest opens across the southern Belt.
sections.bottom_line: Wheat earned its move; beans priced the tour. Corn waits on harvest basis to confirm whether $5.37 holds or fades.
sections.farmer_action: December corn at $5.365: if Friday's window did not move you, this is the same price. Harvest pressure arrives before the September WASDE does.

sections.title: CATTLE: LOW ON THE RANGE, WATCHING AUG 24
sections.body:
- Live cattle closed Friday at $219.25, down half a percent, sitting at just 27% of the 52-week range; feeders at $320.90 mirror that positioning, both far below the summer highs as the market prices returning Mexican feeder supply through the phased Douglas, AZ reopening that began Aug 24.
- The Cargill multi-plant lockout, ongoing since May 19, still removes roughly 6,000 head of daily processing capacity; packer margins remain the binding constraint, not cattle numbers, and that dynamic keeps the box-beef cutout from sending a clear signal to the board.
sections.catalyst: Aug 24 Douglas, AZ port reopening for Mexican feeder cattle began phased restart; Cargill lockout continues to constrain packing capacity.
sections.bottom_line: Cattle are priced for supply returning, not for the lockout resolving. Watch which one blinks first.

sections.title: INPUTS: DIESEL AND PHOSPHATE HEAD INTO HARVEST
sections.body:
- Diesel prices ran to near-record highs heading into harvest, per AgWeb Friday; WTI crude held $83.40, up fractionally, but the diesel crack spread is the number that matters for fieldwork budgets, not the board price on crude.
- CHS and OCP North America announced a $450 million phosphate fertilizer plant in Louisiana, the first domestic phosphate facility in 40 years; it will not relieve 2027 input costs, but it is the structural answer to a supply chain that the Iran-Hormuz cycle, re-escalating in July and now deflating again, exposed as brittle.
sections.catalyst: AgWeb: diesel near-record highs ahead of harvest; CHS/OCP Louisiana phosphate plant announcement confirmed by Agri-Pulse and Farm Policy News.
sections.bottom_line: Diesel is the harvest cost line nobody priced in April. The phosphate plant is a 2028 story, not a 2026 one.

outside_the_pit.title: New DEBT Project Tracks Farm Bankruptcy Trends Nationally
outside_the_pit.body: NASDA and NALC are now compiling Chapter 11 and 12 agricultural bankruptcy filings in a single database. For producers carrying heavy input debt into a tighter-margin year, this is the early-warning system the industry has needed; watch the Q3 filing trend when the first report drops.

outside_the_pit.title: Area Add-On Insurance Uptake Rose Sharply After Subsidy Hike
outside_the_pit.body: A farmdoc daily study found farmers responded strongly after federal premium subsidies on area add-on insurance rose to 80%. With USDA's August yield cuts already in the record and drought expanding in Nebraska and Colorado, the producers who bought the area coverage this spring are sitting on a different risk profile heading into harvest.

the_more_you_know.title: Drought and Basis: The Number Your Elevator Knows Before You Do
the_more_you_know.body: Nebraska drought at 80% coverage means local supplies may be thinner than the state-level yield average implies. Thin crops harvest fast but also store short. Watch your local basis widen into October as country elevators fill unevenly; basis widening before the September WASDE would tell you more about real local supply than any national estimate.

watch_list.desc: Weekly export sales. Wheat above 400K MT confirms the heat-rally demand; beans below 600K MT says the tour premium is priced with no foreign buyer adding to it.
USDA Crop Progress. Corn dough/dent completion and soybean pod-set ratings; any deterioration from last week adds September WASDE premium.
September WASDE. Corn yield at or below 180.7 bu/acre tightens the 1.653B carryout further and validates the December $5.37 hold. Above 182 reopens carry discussion.
Local diesel basis and harvest logistics. Near-record diesel ahead of corn and soybean harvest is an unreported margin hit; lock fuel if you have not.

daily_quote.text: Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished.
